Edwards, M. E., Booker, J. A., Cook, K., Miao, M., Gan, Y., & King, L. A. (2025). Hope as a meaningful emotion: Hope, positive affect, and meaning in life. Emotion, 25(6), 1365.

Feldman, D. B., Shapiro, S. L., & Dreher, D. E. (2026). Mindfulness and hope: distinct yet complementary relationships with psychological well-being. Scientific Reports.16(15398). https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46370-8_reference.pdf

#4742. Is Your Penis Getting Smaller as You Age? This Common Factor Could Hide One to Two Inches.

IT PROBABLY SOUNDS like a nightmare scenario to think your penis is getting shorter. Maybe not even being visible at all. But it can happen as you age, and when it does, doctors refer to it as a buried penis.

Now it's not that your penis is physically getting shorter. It's just that most of it is hidden. More on that below.

CONVINCED YOU LOST an inch? Thankfully, your penis isn’t disappearing; it’s just hidden beneath fat tissue.

Justin Dubin, MD, urologist and men’s health specialist at Baptist Health, says that generally when you can’t see the penis, it’s usually because of low abdominal tissue surrounding the penis.

Essentially, your penis is still its regular size, but it doesn’t extend outside the body. Drogo Montague, MD, a urologist in Ohio tells MH what that looks like. “There is an opening where the penis would normally hang, and the head is usually flush with skin, but there’s no shaft outside of the body.”

Now you don’t just wake up one day with inches of your penis vanished. The effect occurs on a continuum, says Dr. Montague. You might notice at first, for instance, that your penis seems to get shorter and shorter. (Though, this is not the same as the small amount of shrinkage that some men see with age, which is due to skin cells around the penis becoming less elastic.)

“This is a serious condition because it will inhibit urination, intimacy, and personal hygiene,” says Scott Miller, MD, urologist and medical director of Wellstar Urology. “It can also strongly impact self-esteem and overall emotional health.”

MOST CASES OF buried penis are due to one thing: obesity.

While the rates of buried penises haven’t been thoroughly studied, Dr. Montague sees more men in his office today dealing with the issue than he has in the past. His booked-up calendar is no coincidence. The World Health Organization reported that 1 in 7 people is living with obesity. And even though we are living in the golden age of GLP-1s, half of adults worldwide are expected to be overweight or obese by 2050.

The penis itself has two erection chambers. About one-third is inside the body and two-thirds are outside in the penile shaft. When you’re overweight or with severe obesity—and noticing a change in length—what’s changing is basically how much of your penis is inside your body and how much is outside.

“With extreme obesity, it’s like the obese body engulfs the penis. A full buried penis is when the entire penis shaft is buried below the surface of the skin,” says Dr. Montague. So it's still there, but you just can't see it all.

There are a few factors, some starting at birth.

There is a low chance of a baby being born with abnormalities in which the ligaments that attach to the penis are weak. Fortunately, Dr. Dubin says this is usually identified and surgically corrected early on.

Another cause can be “any surgery on your penis” that’s gone wrong, says Dr. Dubin. That includes circumcision, a procedure done on 71.2 percent of American guys are circumcised at birth (or even as an adult). If a doctor does not remove an appropriate amount of foreskin, there is a risk of the penis dropping back into the fatty area surrounding it.

But any procedure that involves the penis runs the risk of scar tissue and possible infection. That includes penile injections and penis enlargement.

“The ironic part is that while a lot of these things try to make your penis look bigger or be bigger, the complication is it can make your penis actually smaller and cause buried penis,” says Dr. Dubin.

Lymphedema can cause swelling in the scrotum. As lymph fluid accumulates, you might see the makings of a buried penis.

Also known as acne inversa, the skin condition can create small and extremely painful lumps under the skin. Lumps usually appear in the armpits, inner thighs, and—you guessed it—your groin. This happens because the body mistakenly attacks hair follicles in the sweat glands, causing pockets of pus and other scarring.

Sometimes when the prostate is removed due to prostate cancer surgery, men may lose about an inch of penile length. “That’s the result of pulling the urethra up to attach to the bladder,” says Dr. Montague. Still, it seems like most penile shortening rebounds as time passes after your surgery, so don't let that stop you from getting your prostate checked.

The condition occurs when scar tissue forms in the penis and it causes a curved erection. The curvature may give the appearance of a shorter length. The issue often arises because of injury to the penis during sex or micro-tears that accumulated from sports or physical accidents affecting the genital area. Fortunately, if diagnosed early, there are drugs and procedures that could straighten out the penis. Read more about it here.

WHEN YOU HAVE a buried penis, certain activities become more difficult. Right away, you might find it hard to pee. Dr. Dubin says guys may not be able to get the stream started and might have poor flow. Buried penis can also cause trouble in the form of dribbling and incontinence.

The area is also tough to clean, which leads to a host of issues that might trigger fungal or bacterial infections or skin breakdown. Buried penis is associated, for example, with a rare skin condition called lichen sclerosus. It’s an inflammatory disorder that causes itchy patches. The skin that hosts these patches becomes very delicate.

Beyond that, penetrative sex remains an ongoing issue. “These men can’t have sex or sex is very difficult,” says Dr. Montague.

Mentally, having a buried penis can cause depression and self-esteem issues. “Most men associate their penis with their masculinity, and they associate fertility with masculinity,” says Dr. Dubin. “These kinds of issues can have strong mental health implications.”

IF YOUR BURIED penis is obesity-related, losing weight will definitely help. But keep in mind that, even after weight loss, you might have excess skin and tissue that keeps your penis buried.

“Sometimes, unfortunately, in very obese people, the damage has already been done, and more aggressive treatment options may be required,” Dr. Dubin. In that scenario, you may need surgery—which is also an option for people who don’t lose weight. Dr. Miller says surgeons would focus on removing the surrounding fat and tissue and repositioning the penis.

“That allows the penis to come outside of the body,” says Dr. Montague. “In most buried penis surgeries, skin and fat are cut out.”

Having a buried penis can be embarrassing to talk about, Dr. Dubin says. It's disturbing to have this happen and it can take a toll on your well-being. If you feel it's getting in the way of living fully, consider talking with a counselor or other mental health professional. It's also crucial to see a doctor if you’re having urinary, hygiene, or sexual health issues because of a buried penis.

Cassie Shortsleeve is a Boston-based journalist with more than a decade of experience reporting for some of the nation's largest print and digital publications, including Women's Health, Men's Health, Medscape, Parents, Conde Nast Traveler, and others. She also writes the best-selling Substack newsletter Two Truths and is a co-founder of the non-profit Chamber of Mothers.

#4741. The Child's Self-Concept: A Social Construct

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

Scientists haven’t found, nor are they likely to find, specific genes that turn on or off and, by doing so, construct the child’s self-concept in a predetermined manner. Absent a purely genetic cause, how does the child develop their self-concept, this crucial entity that delineates the parameters around the child’s needs, their choices, a ceiling on accomplishments, and gauges the child’s interactions with others and life’s smorgasbord of circumstances?

Decades ago, developmental psychologists Alexander, Thomas, and Chess observed that at birth, children come biologically furnished with three innate behavioral predispositions or “temperamental styles”: The “flexible,” adaptive child, the reactive, “feisty,” or not-so-adaptive child, and the “easy,” calm, unhurried child.

Notwithstanding these innate predispositions, how parents welcome, don’t welcome, or otherwise interpret their child’s basic temperament is critical to building the child’s self-concept. For example, a “feisty” child can be seen as a nuisance, irritating, as demanding discipline, and thus reaps parental discouragement or punishment. Or feistiness might be seen as a zest for life, a driving curiosity for novel, stimulating experience, or a precursor to later-life ambition, which would garner parental approval and encouragement—likely accompanied by a few guardrails.

Moreover, the meaning parents impose upon the child’s innate predispositions, and the behavior emanating from them, molds parental attitudes and actions, which, in turn, shapes how the child conceives of themself.

Respected attachment theorist John Bowlby posited that human infants use primitive, inborn cues, like smiling, reaching, cooing, and crying, to elicit nurturing from caregivers, who reciprocate by feeding, comforting, and soothing. These “interactional circuitries” create the fundamentals for a mother-infant attachment bond within the first 18 months of the infant’s life, a time Bowlby called “the sensitive phase.”

When this dyadic bond remains relatively constant and strong over the course of development, the infant or child internalizes a cognitive schema or “working model” of what to expect from subsequent relationships. This bond is the cornerstone of the child’s sense of their worth, the gold standard of their personal standing vis-à-vis others.

For instance, imagine a small child falling, scraping their knee, and crying out in pain, which summons the ministrations of an emotionally attuned mother, who tends to the wound and then follows up with a warm, consoling hug. When reasonably consistent, this type of empathic attunement can be counted upon to nurture maternal trust and the child’s sense of themself as worthy of care. The child’s capacity for interpersonal trust is thus assembled by these early, prototypical interactions, which encourage the child’s prosocial behavior.

The term “person-o-typic affect” (PTA) sounds like a mini-word circus, but a parent’s understanding of the concept can bring significant insight to the relationship they have with their child. Defined literally, PTA refers to the strongest feeling that characteristically surfaces within a parent when in the presence of their child. Despite their strength, parents are often unaware of these feelings; they may be subtle or subconscious, lying outside their immediate awareness. They can also be impossible to ignore, where parents are keenly aware of their presence and the strong influence they wield over their child. But aware or not, these feelings can significantly alter how the parent relates to their child and, consequently, how the child relates to themselves.

For example, a father feels guilty about divorcing his ex-wife because it seemed to shatter his son’s sense of emotional stability. During visitations with his son, guilt warps the father’s behavior through overcompensation, such as granting unearned privileges or turning a blind eye to inappropriate behavior, which are inconsistent with his son’s concept of himself as capable and responsible.

Person-o-typic affect can be an insightful, useful tool for understanding the psychological forces behind parent-child behavior, especially where parental feelings are intense and beg examination. Pertinent questions for parents include: Where do my feelings come from? Do they need modification? How do they influence my behavior and my child’s self-concept?

Need management therapy (NMT) confidently proposes a simple but effective blueprint for building the child’s self-concept. In outline form, it consists of three concrete, doable steps:

1. Need Identification: From the early, seminal moments of life, as loving parents identify their child’s needs, construction of the child’s self-concept begins. And because their needs have been seen by their parents and significant others, the child learns they, too, can identify their own needs and therefore themselves, who they are.

2. Need Legitimization: NMT posits that at their most basic, irreducible level, the child’s needs are valid. For example, the child’s need to be sensitively, respectfully understood is a fundamentally valid need. When the child’s needs are thus “crowned” with validity, a foundation is laid for a positive self-concept. And the child is likely to confidently represent their needs and who they are.

3. Need Representation: Because the child’s basic needs are legitimate, they “demand” representation. Poor or non-management of a legitimate need is inconsistent with building and preserving a complete, healthy self-concept. Under parental mentorship, the child learns to manage their needs by balancing respect for themselves and others, expressing their needs and associated feelings, and measuring the success of these efforts not by how others respond but by how well they represent their needs—difficult but growth-spurring.

By a close adherence to this blueprint, parents can help their child construct a robust self-concept.

Bowlby, J. (`980). Attachment and Loss. Vol. 3, Loss, Sadness and Depression. London: Hogarth Press.

#4740. A Handful of Pistachios May Help You Sleep Better, Review Says

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?

A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.

Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.

While the findings suggest that pistachios may support sleep, the evidence is inconclusive and warrants further study.

“Pistachios are compelling for sleep research because they bring together several nutrients and plant compounds connected to sleep physiology within one whole food,” said study author Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research in the Department of Medicine at Columbia University Institute of Nutrition, in a news release.

“Rather than focusing on a single ‘sleep nutrient,’ this review provides a rationale for studying how the complete pistachio food matrix may affect sleep-related pathways,” she continued.

The narrative review examined existing research on pistachios and sleep-related biology.

The researchers explored whether the combination of nutrients in pistachios could promote quality sleep.

Rather than identifying pistachios as a sleep remedy, the researchers outlined biological pathways through which their nutrients and bioactive compounds might influence sleep.

“We were particularly interested in pistachios because they are particularly high in phytomelatonin, polyphenols, and carotenoids, which we noted were plant-derived components that had been shown to have sleep benefits in preclinical studies,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“We also noted their high content of tryptophan and vitamin B6, which are relevant to melatonin production in humans,” she continued.

Pistachios contain several nutrients associated with sleep, including melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

Other studies examining the effects of some of these nutrients on sleep offer further context.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of tryptophan supplementation found that it may reduce wakefulness after sleep onset, particularly at doses of at least 1 gram (g) daily. However, an ounce of pistachios supplies only about 71 mg, which is much less than the doses examined by the researchers.

Additionally, a 2023 review of dietary polyphenols led by St-Onge identified potential links between plant compounds and sleep outcomes, although results varied across studies.

Neither review established that polyphenols or tryptophan from pistachios specifically affected sleep quality.

“I was not surprised that pistachios may help support sleep, given their combination of nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” said Michelle Routhenstein, MS, a preventive cardiology dietitian at EntirelyNourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“Pistachios provide tryptophan, an amino acid the body uses to produce serotonin and melatonin; vitamin B6, which supports these pathways; and magnesium, which plays a role in nervous system function and sleep regulation,” she told Healthline.

The new review highlights the concept of the “food matrix,” or how nutrients and bioactive compounds interact within a whole food.

Instead of investigating tryptophan, magnesium, or melatonin individually, researchers were curious about the combined effects of consuming them together in pistachios.

Laboratory and simulated-digestion research offers clues about how fiber and plant compounds in pistachios and peanuts interact with gut microbes. However, these findings do not establish that eating pistachios changes sleep quality in real-world conditions.

Broader nutrition research also points to a relationship between diet and sleep.

A 2021 review in the Annual Review of Nutrition examined evidence linking dietary patterns and individual nutrients to sleep outcomes. The findings suggest a relationship between sleep and diet, but note that more research is needed to determine cause and effect.

In a nutshell, the current evidence builds a compelling case for pistachios as a sleep aid.

However, it’s too soon to recommend pistachios as a sleep remedy, as many factors may affect sleep quality and insomnia.

“Sleep difficulties can have different underlying causes,” Routhenstein noted. “If inadequate intake of these nutrients is a contributing factor, pistachios may help, but they may not address sleep issues related to other nutrient deficiencies or other causes.”

Much of the supporting evidence cited in the review comes from studies of individual nutrients, other foods, laboratory experiments, or biological mechanisms rather than from trials involving whole pistachios.

Researchers have also reported significant variations in the melatonin content of pistachios, making the amount in a typical serving difficult to pinpoint.

Additionally, the review received support from American Pistachio Growers, and the corresponding author, St-Onge, serves on its advisory board. Larger studies and clinical trials are needed, ideally without industry funding, to ensure well-rounded results.

Indeed, the authors call for randomized controlled trials examining whether eating pistachios affects sleep outcomes, including sleep quality, duration, and melatonin levels.

“This was a review; we noted that the complete profile of pistachios would make them well-suited to support healthful sleep, but research is needed to evaluate this,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“This is the next step, and something we are actively working on. We also need to better understand what dosage and frequency of consumption would be optimal.”

Regardless, a handful of pistachios is still considered a healthy choice as part of a balanced diet.

“A small handful, about 1 ounce of shelled pistachios, is an appropriate portion,” Routhenstein said. “Enjoy them during the day or as a light afternoon or evening snack when you’re hungry.”

If nutrients like tryptophan help promote sleep, it’s possible that other nuts could yield similar results.

“Other nuts, such as almonds and walnuts, may offer similar benefits because they also contain nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” Routhenstein said.

“Early research is encouraging, but it’s too soon to say how much they might help.”

Other foods, like turkey, also contain tryptophan.

“For someone allergic to nuts, foods such as tofu, beans, oats, eggs, dairy, and fish can provide tryptophan, which the body uses to make serotonin and melatonin,” Routhenstein said. “The goal is to meet their nutrient needs rather than rely on one food to improve sleep.”

Sleep health depends on multiple factors. As such, Routhenstein recommends a personalized approach to getting better sleep, from what you eat and when you eat to addressing any nutritional gaps.

“I would also encourage regular, balanced meals throughout the day to support blood sugar management, especially for those with diabetes, while avoiding large meals close to bedtime,” Routhenstein said. “Caffeine later in the day and alcohol in the evening are also worth considering as possible sleep disruptors.”

#4739. The 2027 Lexus RZ starts at under $50,000 and offers over 300 miles of range

The 2027 Lexus RZ will begin arriving at dealerships early next year, with prices starting at under $50,000.

After introducing the updated RZ last year, the electric SUV has seen significantly more demand this year.

Toyota’s luxury brand sold over 10,000 RZs through September, nearly double (+91%) the 5,340 it managed during the same period last year.

For the 2027 model year, the Lexus RZ will be available with three powertrains: 350e, 450e AWD, and 550e F Sport AWD.

The base 350e uses a 79.6 kWh battery and a 221-horsepower front motor, delivering up to 301 miles of electric range.

Upgrading to the 450e AWD model costs an extra $3,500 and starts at $50,995. The AWD variant also uses the 79.6 kWh battery but adds a rear motor with Lexus’ DIRECT4 all-wheel-drive, delivering a combined 308 horsepower and 260 miles of range.

The top-spec Lexus RZ 550e AWD starts at $58,770. The AWD setup delivers a combined 402 horsepower, which Lexus said enables it to sprint from 0 to 60 mph in 4.2 seconds, the fastest of the lineup.

The F Sport variant is also the first to feature M Mode, an electronic system that replicates the feeling of an eight-speed manual transmission.

All variants have a built-in NACS port on the passenger side, so drivers can use Tesla Superchargers without a separate adaptor. Charging the battery from 10% to 80% takes about 30 minutes.

Inside, the RZ comes with NuLuxe-trimmed seats as standard, while the Luxury and F Sport grades have Ultrasuede-trimmed seats and laser-etched Ultrasuede door trim inserts.

All 2027 RZ models also include a heated steering wheel and heated and ventilated front seats as standard.

Introducing the 2014? Lexus RZ. AWD...308 horsepower and 260 miles of range... 10-80% fast charging at an average speed of 112 kw.

Toyota may not know how to make an EV, but it is nailing this time travel thing.

The 2027 RZ comes with the latest Lexus Interface multimedia system, including a 14″ navigation screen with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

Lexus said the 2027 RZ will begin arriving at dealerships early next year. Starting at $47,495, the RZ is $7,500 more than the Tesla Model Y ($39,990), which offers up to 321 miles of range.

#4737. The Value of Appreciation

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

Which is worth more: a million dollars today or a penny that doubles each day for 30 days?

At first, the million looks like the obvious choice.

The penny begins at one cent on day one and doubles each day afterward. By day 10, the balance is a measly $5.12. By day 20, the balance reaches a meager $5,242.88. By day 30, it reaches $5,368,709.12, more than five times the lump sum.

That is the power of compounding. Small beginnings can be easy to underestimate; early progress can look almost insignificant.

Everyday life also offers valuable moments that are easy to overlook: a small gesture of kindness, a moment of connection worth savoring, a heartfelt moment of gratitude.

These are psychological pennies: small acts of appreciation that are easy to take for granted but are worth repeating in pursuit of the good life. The invitation is to make appreciation a regular practice, rather than reserve it for one extraordinary occasion.What people usually think of as extraordinary is not likely to happen every day. Small reasons for gratitude offer more frequent opportunities to experience the benefits of appreciation. Waiting for something extraordinary can lead people to overlook the value already present in their lives.

Psychologists Mitchel Adler and Nancy Fagley define appreciation as “acknowledging the value and meaning of something—an event, a person, a behavior, an object—and feeling a positive emotional connection to it.” They identify eight aspects of appreciation, including gratitude, appreciation of the present moment, and awe.In finance, appreciation means an increase in value. A home or stock portfolio appreciates when its price rises.

The connection is a useful metaphor for psychological wealth. Recognizing value can increase the value people experience. An ordinary conversation with a friend can feel richer when someone recognizes the gift of having that person in their life. An ordinary afternoon can feel extraordinary when a person pauses to appreciate being alive and the opportunity to spend time with someone they love. In this sense, recognizing the value already present in relationships and experiences can increase how rich life feels.

In a 2012 study of 243 participants, psychologist Nancy Fagley found that appreciation was associated with greater life satisfaction. Awe offers one way to practice appreciation in ordinary life. Awe involves a sense of vastness that challenges a person’s usual understanding of the world.A person does not necessarily need to visit the Grand Canyon or the Himalayas to experience awe. Someone might pause to consider the complexity of a living tree, witness an act of kindness, or feel a profound sense of wonder at a heart that keeps beating without conscious instruction.

In a small randomized study, psychologist Virginia Sturm and colleagues asked adults to take weekly 15-minute outdoor walks for eight weeks. One group also received instructions to approach their surroundings with wonder and seek out novelty. Compared with the control group, which received the walking assignment without those additional instructions, those encouraged to seek wonder and novelty reported greater increases over time in daily positive emotions involving connection with others.

To practice appreciation more consistently, choose a familiar activity and consider a more appreciative lens through which to view it.

Give one person your full attention. During a conversation with a friend or loved one, set aside distractions and appreciate the opportunity to spend time together. Listen with interest. When appropriate, let them know you are glad to have them in your life.

Reconsider something familiar. During a routine moment, notice something that is easy to take for granted. At a meal, that might be the nourishment the food provides, the people who made the meal possible, or the pleasure of tasting something you enjoy.

Take a walk with curiosity. During a walk, look closely at something you would usually pass by. Consider the complexity of a living tree, for example, or the scale of the sky above it. Allow time for curiosity and wonder.

The penny that began at one cent reaches $5.37 million by day 30. Psychological pennies can be just as easy to overlook, and compounding them over time may increase your psychological wealth. Small, ordinary moments can be worth doubling down on. Recognizing the value already present in such moments can increase how rich life feels.The practical idea is to return to such moments throughout the day and appreciate them more fully, rather than postpone appreciation until something extraordinary happens. There is no guaranteed rate of return in life satisfaction, but there are good reasons to invest consistently over the long run.

Those are investments that can be made today, and made again tomorrow.

#4736. ACOG Strongly Recommends Hormone Therapy for Menopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) published updated recommendations for menopause management in Obstetrics & Gynecology on October 15.

These expanded recommendations are the most comprehensive guidance to date. They include new clinical guidelines for menopause hormone therapy (MHT), nonhormonal medications, and nonpharmacological treatment of vasomotor symptoms (VMS), which include hot flashes and night sweats, and sleep and mood changes.

According to the ACOG guidance, 50%–92% of females experiencing menopause report VMS.

Around 16%–66% of females in the United States report menopause-related sleep issues, and more than one-third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal females report experiencing depressive symptoms.

“In recent years, misconceptions about the risks of hormone therapy have been widespread, which has made some clinicians reluctant to prescribe it and some patients hesitant to use it,” Bruce Pier, MD, clinical professor and associate fellowship director at the University of North Carolina and collaborator on the ACOG clinical practice guidelines, told Healthline.

“This guidance offers a comprehensive review of the evidence to support individualized counseling and shared decision making. Our hope is that it clears up those misconceptions and expands access to treatment.”

The ACOG is also developing companion guidance for genitourinary syndrome of menopause, expected in 2027.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of MHT with estrogen and progestogens (or estrogen alone for people without a uterus) for both VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbance, in individuals who can use hormones.

It also conditionally recommends conjugated estrogen plus bazedoxifene (Duavee) as an alternative for these issues.

According to a meta-analysis from 2021 that was cited by the guidelines, estrogen therapy, with or without progestogens, significantly reduced VMS frequency and severity compared to a placebo or no treatment. A 2017 meta-analysis ranked transdermal estradiol plus a progestogen as the most effective option for reducing VMS frequency.

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis, also cited by the guidelines, found that MHT was associated with improved self-reported sleep quality. Once again, transdermal therapies showed some of the largest effects.

The ACOG recommends initiating MHT before age 60 or within 10 years of the onset of natural menopause..

It also suggests that the decision to start MHT for VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances should be based on a shared decision making discussion about an individual’s symptoms and the benefits and risks of therapy. Consideration should also be taken regarding an individual’s:

Research shows that factors such as race, culture, socioeconomic status, gender identity, and sexual orientation can influence how individuals experience menopause and the care they receive.

According to the SWAN study, Black women reported more menopause symptoms than white women but were less likely to be treated for them.

“This updated document shines a light on these inequities. Clinicians can proactively help right now by asking every patient in midlife about symptoms, rather than waiting for them to bring it up. Long term, we hope this document drives more research funding to understand these gaps and begin closing them,” said Pier.

The ACOG stated in the guidelines that, “The available evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against the use of estrogen–progestogen or estrogen-only MHT for the treatment of menopause-related depressive symptoms.”

It recommends that perimenopausal and postmenopausal individuals who meet the diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD) or those whose most noticeable symptom is depression should be treated according to depression management guidelines.

Current treatment guidelines for depression include therapy, medication, or a combination of the two.

Psychological treatments for depression include psychotherapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), while antidepressants are among the most commonly prescribed medications.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) for the management of menopausal symptoms like VMS and depression in individuals who don’t want to use MHT or can’t use it.

Currently, paroxetine is the only antidepressant that is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the management of VMS.

The ACOG also strongly recommends the use of neurokinin receptor antagonists to manage VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances in people who don’t desire hormone therapy or can’t use it.

There are currently two neurokinin receptor antagonists approved by the FDA to manage menopause symptoms. Fezolinetant (Veozah) was approved in 2023 to help manage hot flashes. In 2025, the FDA approved elinzanetant (LYNKUET) for the management of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause.

Another nonhormonal treatment for VMS that the ACOG conditionally recommends is gabapentin.

There are various nonpharmacologic treatments that the ACOG conditionally recommends for the management of VMS, vasomotor-related sleep disturbances, and mood changes. These are treatments that don’t involve the use of medications.

The nonpharmacologic treatments conditionally recommended include:

It is generally recommended that these interventions are used alongside hormonal or nonhormonal medications.

The ACOG noted that there is not enough evidence to support the efficacy or safety of phytoestrogens, such as soy isoflavones, or herbal supplements, which are not regulated by the FDA in the same way medications are for safety, purity, or efficacy.

“Menopause is finally getting the attention it deserves, and this document shows what evidence-based care should look like in this space. It lays out a range of safe, effective options for managing menopause symptoms. My message to anyone struggling with these symptoms is simple: talk to your clinician. You don’t have to suffer through them,” said Pier.

#4735. BMW’s new iX5 looks like a big upgrade next to the old X5 [Images]

BMW’s new iX5 is hard to miss with its distinct Double-X headlights. Here’s how it stacks up against the outgoing X5, side by side.

The X5 is among BMW’s best-selling vehicles in the US. In its fifth generation, it will be available across five powertrains.

In the US, it will be offered in gas, plug-in hybrid (PHEV), and, for the first time, battery electric (EV) powertrains. Other markets will also see diesel and hydrogen fuel cell variants.

The gas-powered 2027 X5 40 xDrive is now available, starting at $72,100, but the electric iX5 won’t go on sale until November.

Ahead of its official launch next month, Bimmertoday posted several images of the new iX5 parked next to the outgoing X5 G05, giving us a good side-by-side comparison.

Although it still looks like an X5, the new iX5 stands apart with BMW’s Neue Klasse design. The new upright, slimmer BMW Kidney Grille replaces the old wide, chunkier grille design.

A post shared by bimmertoday (@bimmertoday)

You can also see BMW’s new “double-X” light signature, which combines the headlights, daytime running lights, side lights, and turn signals into one unit. The Double-X headlights come standard, but BMW said you can turn them off for simpler diagonal stripes.

The new BMW iX5 60 xDrive will go on sale in the US next month. Using a 144 kWh battery, BMW said the electric SUV will offer up to 435 miles of range.

Last week, BMW showcased the i5’s fast-charging capabilities for the first time during a media event in Southern California with IONNA and Alpitronic. During the event, the iX5 60 xDrive hit a peak of 464 kW, which BMW said enables it to add up to 170 miles of range in 10 minutes.

The iX5 is powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, delivering a combined 578 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft of torque. BMW says it can go from 0 to 60 mph in 4.4 seconds and tow up to 6,000 lbs.

Love this. If I were in the market for a new vehicle this would not just be on the list, it would be the list. With 450 miles of range, fast charging that adds 300 miles in 20 minutes, outstanding reviews for ride quality, cabin silence, L2++ ADAS, etc. it is the benchmark for EVs in America. Glad to see BMW bringing the A game and glad that someone is building a world class EV in America.

Inside, the iX5 adopts BMW’s Neue Klasse design, which includes a 17.9″ navigation touchscreen and the new BMW Panoramic Vision that stretches across the bottom of the windshield. Buyers can opt to add the optional 14.6″ passenger screen for a third display.

BMW’s new iX5 is 197.2″ long, 78.7″ wide, and 68.9″ tall, or about the size of the Porsche Cayenne Electric.

BMW will open orders for the new iX5 60 xDrive in November, starting at $79,800. It will be BMW’s first electric vehicle built in the US. Production is set to begin at its Plant Spartanburg in South Carolina by the end of the year.

#4734. It's So Much More Than Used Clothing

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

When I thought of Goodwill, I pictured used clothing. Then I toured its Miami-Dade facility and learned so much more.

Goodwill Industries of South Florida helps people with disabilities and other employment barriers gain greater independence through job training, employment, and placement services. According to president and CEO David Landsberg, it is Florida’s largest employer of people with disabilities and the 18th-largest employer in South Florida.

Its businesses include manufacturing military and other apparel, providing custodial services to federal workplaces, and operating a commercial laundry. They also provide career training in fields such as HVAC and solar installation and place graduates in community positions.

I was particularly moved by the employees making American flags for veterans’ burials. These flags will cover caskets for our veterans. I watched a blind man sew with remarkable precision and speed.

I saw enthusiasm and pride throughout the tour, especially during a Spirit of Goodwill Band rehearsal. The musicians, who work at Goodwill and have a variety of disabilities, were superb. They are given time during the workweek to practice, and they perform at community functions, including the organization’s fundraising gala.

Many of us carry disability insurance in case illness or injury prevents us from working. But what about someone born with a disability, or who developed one in childhood, who has never had the opportunity to work?

The World Health Organization’s 2022 guidelines recognize meaningful work as a source of confidence, accomplishment, and inclusion. Work gives our days structure, with tasks to complete and opportunities to grow. A conversation over lunch or someone asking how our weekend went may seem trivial until those interactions are missing, as many of us discovered during the pandemic.

As a parent who has spent decades advocating for my daughter and worrying about her future, I know how deeply reassuring it is to see an adult child take on work responsibilities and form relationships outside the family.

The Americans with Disabilities Act protects equal opportunity among qualified people with disabilities. Employers with 15 or more employees should not discriminate and should provide reasonable accommodations if the applicant can meet the job's qualifications. Yet, too many are unemployed.

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, in 2025, the unemployment rate among people with disabilities ages 16 and older was 8.3 percent, compared with 4.1 percent among those without disabilities. Among people ages 16 to 64 with a disability, just 41.8 percent were working or looking for work in 2025.

Eileen Grubba, a disability activist, award-winning actress, writer, and producer, shared with me her valuable perspective: “Those with disabilities often have the most to offer. They have survived the unthinkable. We rarely consider what they handle every single day, and what they’ve learned because of it. We need to open our minds and turn to those who know best how to adapt, adjust, and overcome, simply because they’ve been overcoming all their lives."

Goodwill’s founder, Edgar J. Helms, expressed the organization’s guiding idea: “Not charity, but a chance.”

I left the tour thinking how little I knew about workplace accommodations and how heartwarming it is to see others succeed.

You might contact your local Goodwill or another employment organization and ask whether you can visit. A lot can be achieved through training, time, and connection.

#4733. Tesla appears to be preparing to sell US-built Model 3s in Canada again

Tesla Canada has updated the Model 3 Premium Rear-Wheel Drive on its website with 584 km of range and a 0-100 km/h time of 5.2 seconds. Those are the exact specs of the Fremont-built Long Range RWD that Tesla sold in Canada two years ago.

The Shanghai-built version, the $39,490 CAD car Canadians haven’t been able to order since early October, is rated at 463 km and 6.2 seconds. The new numbers point to a different car from a different factory.

Canadian Tesla owner RJ was first to spot the change on X:

Tesla Canada 🇨🇦 has updated Model 3 Premium RWD range and 0-100 specs.New specs:584 km range (previously 463 km)0-100 in 5.2 seconds (previously 6.2 seconds)Note: Premium Model 3 RWD orders are currently paused because the Government of Canada states Tesla has exhausted its… pic.twitter.com/PeWP15w2RS

The new figures are in the “Model 3 Premium Specs” section of Tesla’s Canadian Model 3 page, under the Rear-Wheel Drive tab, along with a curb weight of 1,745 kg. The page’s marketing copy now also promises “up to 584 km (EPA est.) on a single charge.”

Tesla hasn’t touched its Canadian comparison page, though. As of this afternoon, it still lists the Model 3 Premium RWD at 463 km, 6.2 seconds and $39,490.

In October 2024, Tesla Canada listed the Model 3 Long Range RWD at 584 km and 5.2 seconds, starting at $54,990 and eligible for the federal iZEV rebate. That car came from Fremont.

They also line up with the Model 3 Premium RWD Tesla sells in the US today. Tesla’s US website rates it at 363 miles of EPA range, which converts to 584 km, with 0-60 mph in 4.9 seconds. It starts at $42,490 USD.

There’s one other candidate. Giga Shanghai builds a Model 3 Long Range RWD for the Chinese market with a 78.4 kWh pack, 830 km of CLTC range and the same 5.2-second 0-100 km/h time.

But a Shanghai-built car runs into the same quota problem that paused Model 3 orders in Canada earlier this month. Tesla’s website says orders will resume “if Govt of Canada issues more quota, expected March 2027.” Meanwhile, the federal tracker showed 33,069 of the period’s permits still unused as of October 9.

So if Tesla wants to sell a long-range Model 3 in Canada before March, it has to come from Fremont.

And that’s where it gets expensive. Canada’s 25% counter-tariffs on US-made vehicles, in place since April 2025, still apply. The Department of Finance’s counter-tariff page, updated October 9, says the measures against US autos “continue to apply.”

Those tariffs are what pushed Tesla out of US-built Model 3s in the first place. When they hit, Tesla raised the Model 3 Long Range AWD by $11,000 to $79,990 and dropped the $55,990 RWD entirely. In March, it shipped its remaining US-built Model 3 inventory out of Canada ahead of the switch to Shanghai, which led to the record-low $39,490 Model 3 Premium RWD in May.

If Tesla applies a similar markup to a Fremont-built Premium RWD, it would land somewhere around $65,000 to $67,000. That’s well above the $50,000 transaction cap of Canada’s new $5,000 EV Affordability Program, even though US-built cars otherwise qualify through CUSMA (Chinese-built ones don’t).

Right now, the only Model 3 you can order in Canada is the Performance, which Tesla priced at $74,990 when it cut its price in May.

Do Canadians really want to buy from a guy helping the trade war against Canada? I hope not.

Tesla hasn’t announced anything, and the configurator hasn’t changed. But Tesla doesn’t usually rewrite a spec sheet for a car it isn’t planning to sell, and these numbers match a car it has sold in Canada before.

The most logical explanation is a stopgap. Tesla had a real hit with the $39,490 Model 3, ran through its quota in about four months, and is now stuck selling a $75,000 Performance until March. A Fremont-built Premium RWD would give buyers a long-range Model 3 at something less painful than that.

The problem is that it’d be a tough sell. I think Canadian buyers are more likely to wait and see if Tesla gets more quotas next and year. At the same time, they will wait to see what the Chinese automakers have to offer next year.

#4732. Christina Applegate ‘Not Happy at All’ After Learning She Was Misdiagnosed With MS

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Christina Applegate shared an unexpected health update on her return to the MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.

The two actors have detailed their experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS), a neurological disorder that can lead to debilitating symptoms affecting daily functioning and quality of life.

Applegate, 54, has been raising awareness about the condition since her initial diagnosis in 2021.

In two podcast episodes released October 20, Applegate revealed that doctors had told her she was misdiagnosed with MS.

“She came into my room and said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS,’ ” Applegate said as she fought back tears. “I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy.”

The “Anchorman” and “Dead to Me” actor explained that her symptoms have continued to worsen, leaving her without an explanation for what she’s experiencing as doctors investigate the cause.

Being misdiagnosed with MS is relatively common. Applegate’s revelation highlights a difficult reality for people living with unexplained symptoms resembling MS. Her experience raises questions about how MS is diagnosed, why misdiagnoses may occur, and what people can do when their symptoms don’t match their diagnosis.

While MS can be difficult to diagnose, an accurate diagnosis can help people with the condition gain access to appropriate treatment. A misdiagnosis, on the other hand, may lead to unnecessary interventions and medication, and take an emotional toll over time.

“MS can be challenging to diagnose because there is no single test that confirms it in every case,” said Steve Allder, MD, consultant neurologist at Re:Cognition Health.

“An incorrect diagnosis can have significant consequences. Someone incorrectly diagnosed with MS may experience considerable anxiety, undergo unnecessary investigations, or receive treatments with potential risks and side effects. Equally, if MS is missed, treatment may be delayed, potentially allowing further neurological damage,” Allder told Healthline.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis underscores that MS misdiagnoses remain a concern.

Research suggests that around 15% of people diagnosed with MS may actually have another condition.

However, estimates vary across studies, with some reporting rates ranging from 5–41%.

While an accurate diagnosis can guide patients toward appropriate treatment, a mistaken one may lead to unnecessary medication, emotional distress, and years of uncertainty.

New diagnostic guidelines offer hope for greater accuracy, but they also raise important questions about how doctors can adequately distinguish MS from other conditions.

“Research has shown that MS can be both overdiagnosed and underdiagnosed,” Allder said.

“Diagnosis relies on a combination of symptoms, neurological examination, MRI findings, and sometimes, additional tests. It is also important to recognize that diagnoses can evolve as new evidence emerges. As neurologists, we must remain open to revisiting a diagnosis when symptoms or test results do not fit, ensuring patients receive appropriate treatment and support.”

MS symptoms may vary widely and overlap with several other conditions. These may include:

Because these conditions share certain features with MS, healthcare professionals should consider a patient’s full clinical profile rather than relying on a single symptom or scan.

“MS can cause numbness, tingling, muscle weakness, visual disturbances, balance problems, and fatigue. However, these symptoms are not unique to the condition,” Allder said.

“For example, numbness and tingling may indicate peripheral neuropathy, sometimes associated with diabetes or vitamin B12 deficiency. Weakness or altered sensation may result from a trapped nerve or spinal cord compression. Migraines can cause visual disturbances and sensory symptoms, while inner-ear disorders may affect balance,” he continued.

Allder noted that fatigue is particularly nonspecific and may be associated with:

He explained that, as a neurologist, he considers the pattern, duration, and progression of symptoms alongside examination findings.

“No single symptom automatically indicates MS. A thorough assessment is essential to identify the underlying cause and ensure the patient receives appropriate treatment,” he said.

There is no single test that definitively confirms every case of MS.

Diagnosis typically involves reviewing symptoms, conducting neurological examinations, and evaluating MRI scans and laboratory results.

MRI findings may be tricky to interpret. Some white-matter spots resemble MS lesions but may result from migraine, aging, or other conditions. Misapplying diagnostic criteria or overlooking alternative explanations can also lead to mistakes.

“MRI abnormalities alone do not confirm MS,” Allder said. “The diagnosis must be based on the overall clinical picture, with alternative explanations carefully considered.”

Research also suggests that MS misdiagnosis rates may differ by sex.

Research shows females are 2.1 times more likely to be misdiagnosed with MS than males, highlighting the potential for diagnostic bias and differences in how symptoms are evaluated.

The updated MS diagnostic criteria published in 2025 offer a framework for improving diagnosis.

The updated guidelines introduce several important changes.

For instance, the optic nerve (the nerve connecting the eye to the brain) is now included as a fifth anatomical location for assessing evidence of MS.

The revised criteria also include new MRI biomarkers, such as the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions. These features can help doctors distinguish MS-related abnormalities from other conditions.

These changes may help doctors diagnose MS earlier and more accurately.

If you experience persistent or recurring neurological symptoms, seek medical advice. Your doctor can assess your symptoms and, if applicable, refer you to a neurologist.

Sudden weakness, vision loss, or difficulty speaking requires urgent medical assessment, Allder said.

“Depending on the findings, investigations may include MRI scans of the brain and spinal cord, blood tests, and, in some cases, a lumbar puncture,” Allder noted.

“It is important that results are interpreted alongside symptoms and examination findings, as no single test should determine the diagnosis in isolation.”

Allder said that if you’re unsure about a diagnosis, you can ask your neurologist what evidence supports it and whether alternative health conditions have been considered.

“A second opinion or follow-up assessment may be appropriate. The priority is an accurate diagnosis that leads to the right treatment and support,” Allder said.

#4731. 6 stellar images of the early universe

Published Oct 25, 2026 8:01 PM EDT

Millions of miles away from Earth, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and Nancy Roman Space Telescope are revealing the early days of our vast universe in extraordinary detail. A team at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian have developed Lumina, one of the largest and most detailed simulations ever created of the early universe.

The new model is detailed in a study published today in the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society. It recreates how ordinary matter, dark matter, and radiation all interacted during the universe’s first 2 billion years. This gives scientists a new tool to test out their theories about how the cosmos evolved after the big bang. Comparing observations from JWST, Roman, and other telescopes with Lumina’s predictions, also can help astronomers determine whether their understanding of the laws governing our universe remain accurate or if new discoveries require them to reconsider existing theories.

Creating Lumina required more than 15,000 graphics processing units. Take a peak at some of Lumina’s stellar images and videos in the gallery below. (Click to expand images to full screen.)

“With JWST, the early universe has become an exciting new frontier in astrophysics,” study lead author Oliver Zier, a computation astronomer and ITC Fellow at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, said in a statement. “To understand what we are seeing with this telescope, we need to translate our theories into detailed predictions. After several years of work, with plenty of ups and downs, it is incredibly rewarding to see the simulation results and watch our predictions come to life in video.”

Lumina is the largest cosmological radiation-hydrodynamics simulation ever created. This kind of simulation models how the universe’s fundamental ingredients interact to form stars and galaxies. These ingredients include dark matter, light, and gas. Lumina is tracing how the earliest galaxies emerged and transformed the vast regions of gas between them over the universe’s first 2 billion years.

“We feel incredibly fortunate to be building simulations like Lumina,” added Aaron Smith, an assistant professor of physics at the University of Texas at Dallas and study co-author. “For the first time, we can follow along as both hydrogen and helium changed into their modern form across such an enormous volume of the universe, while still resolving the galaxies and other luminous objects driving that transformation.”

To view the entire project, visit the Lumina Project.

#4730. In 1934, a doctor brought a dog back to life. He tried to do the same with humans.

Published Oct 26, 2026 9:02 AM EDT

Under the harsh glare of overhead lights at a laboratory at the University of California at Berkeley, Lazarus II lay motionless.

Dr. Robert E. Cornish, who’d asphyxiated the rangy white fox terrier with ether and nitrogen, watched the clock. Six minutes after the final heartbeat, the scientist gathered up the dog and strapped him to a teeterboard, a see-saw-like invention whose back-and-forth, up-and-down motion Cornish believed was key to restoring the blood’s circulation.

He pushed a saline solution primed with oxygen, heart-stimulating adrenalin, and the liver extract heparin into a vein in Lazarus’ thigh, then lowered his head over the patient. As his assistant rocked the teeterboard and rubbed the little body vigorously, Cornish exhaled deep breaths into the dog’s mouth and lungs.

Long seconds turned to minutes and then, suddenly, Lazarus gasped and jerked his leg. Slowly, his heart began to beat. Lazarus II had returned from the dead.

With the invention of modern cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) still a quarter century off, resurrecting Lazarus after his heart stopped was something of a miracle in 1934. But while the fox terrier lived for another eight hours and 13 minutes, he did not live well, stuck in a restless zombie state punctuated by the occasional whine, bark, and panting.

“Irreversible damage occurs to either the heart or the brain after a period of time, making a good recovery impossible,” Samuel Tisherman, professor of surgery and director for the Center for Critical Care and Trauma Education at the University of Maryland, Baltimore, tells Popular Science.

Lazarus II wasn’t Cornish’s first attempt to revive dying patients using his teeterboard. He wasn’t even the first Lazarus. The young scientist, a former child prodigy who’d earned his doctorate from UC Berkeley at age 22, became obsessed with resuscitation sometime around 1933.

Before working on dogs, Cornish began his reanimating work on people. A 62-year-old printer who died of cardiac arrest was the first to receive Cornish’s reanimation treatment. Four-and-a-half hours after his death, Cornish arrived at the hospital to strap the man’s heating pad-swaddled body to a teeterboard. After see-sawing the patient up and down for 90 minutes, Cornish failed to revive the subject—although Cornish noted a point at which the printer’s “face seemed to warm up suddenly, sparkle returned to the eyes, and soft pulsations were observed in the soft tissue between windpipe and sternum,” according to science journalist Frank Swain’s How to Make a Zombie: The Life (and Death) Science of Reanimation and Mind Control.

Two weeks later, Cornish tried the same treatment on a 22-year-old machinist who’d been pulled dead from the San Francisco Bay three hours before, working his body on the teeterboard for a full four hours. It, too, failed, along with a third attempt the following day in which Cornish submerged an electrocuted cadaver in a warm bath instead of using heating pads before placing the body on the teeterboard.

Dissatisfied with the outcomes, Cornish decided it would be wise to perfect his methodology on fox terriers before returning to human subjects. He named each one Lazarus after the biblical man Jesus brought back to life.

Cornish’s biggest breakthrough came with Lazarus IV. Though blind and unable to stand on its own, within 13 days the dog could crawl, bark, and sit up. Its appetite, too, had returned. Over the few months of his life after death, Lazarus IV went through almost a pound of meat each day.

The next patient, Lazarus V, recovered even more quickly. It took just four days for the dog to resume some normal behaviors despite suffering blindness and brain damage. Like his predecessor, he too lived only a few months.

Despite their mixed outcome, Cornish was praised for his Lazarus experiments. In the press, the scientist who’d often been considered an oddball by his peers for pursuing projects like underwater reading glasses was hailed as a celebrity. A movie about his work, Life Returns, was released in 1935.

But Cornish’s resuscitation experiments were not without controversy. Dogged by animal rights protests and other outcries from the public, UC Berkeley’s administrators had him removed from campus. Cornish continued his work from home, turning a garden shed into a laboratory that neighbors claimed stunk up the street.

The science behind resuscitating a dying patient has come a long way since the Lazarus experiments. These days, “how to restore a pulse depends upon the cause of the cardiac arrest,” says Tisherman.

“The first, most important intervention is assuring good chest compressions,” he continues.

How quickly intervention begins also plays a role. “It’s generally been considered that if the period of no blood flow at all, before someone starts CPR, is greater than five minutes, the outcome will likely be poor,” says Tisherman—though that idea has been challenged and “no one knows for sure.”

While drugs and medications similar to those used by Cornish to improve blood flow and return heart rhythms to normal in his Lazarus experiments play a part in modern resuscitation protocol, emergency medical practitioners have never adopted the teeterboard he believed was key to restoring life.

Cornish never had the opportunity to prove that his teeterboard worked, despite appealing to the governors of Nevada, Arizona, and Colorado for permission to revive criminals executed by the gas chamber shortly after completing his Lazarus experiments. Their refusal didn’t stop Cornish from making one final attempt in 1948, sending multiple requests to the warden at San Quentin State Prison to resuscitate kidnapper and murderer Thomas McMonigle following his upcoming execution by gas chamber—all of which were rebuffed.

Once news of Cornish’s plan for McMonigle became public, more than 50 other “mostly single men” volunteered to be brought back to life by his teeterboard but by then, it seems, Cornish had moved on to something a little less extraordinary: formulating and marketing toothpaste to the American public.

#4729. The 2027 Kia EV6 is over $8,000 more than the new EV3

Kia announced that 2027 EV6 prices start at about $38,000, or $8,000 more than the new EV3.

The 2027 Kia EV6 arrives as a carryover model from last year. After reducing prices on the 2026 model year by $5,000 just a few months ago, the 2027 EV6 remains the same price across all trims.

The base EV6 Light standard-range RWD model starts at $37,900, not including the $1,545 destination fee, which is the same as last year.

Powered by a 63 kWh battery, the standard-range variant offers up to 237 miles of range. Upgrading to the EV6 Light long range RWD model costs an extra $3,300, starting at $41,200, but delivers up to 319 miles of range using a larger 84 kWh battery.

The 84 kWh battery offers up to 319 miles of range in RWD variants, while AWD EV6 models get up to 295 miles. The top-spec EV6 GT-Line AWD has up to 270 miles of range.

Kia said that with the EV6 MSRP unchanged and the launch of the new EV3, it’s “making EVs more attainable for those who embrace the fully electric lifestyle.”

The 2027 Kia EV3 starts at just $29,890, or about $8,000 less than the EV6. Kia’s entry-level electric SUV is available in five trims: Light, Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT.

The lowest-priced EV3 Light FWD model uses a 58.3 kWh battery and delivers an EPA-estimated range of up to 221 miles.

Higher-priced trims, including the Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT, use a larger 81.4 kWh battery that delivers up to 321 miles of range on a single charge. Like the EV6, the EV3 is also available with front-wheel-drive and all-wheel-drive powertrain options.

Inside, both the EV6 and EV3 feature Kia’s ccNC infotainment system. The setup includes nearly 30″ of screen space in a curved panoramic display, including dual 12.3″ instrument cluster and central navigation screens, plus a 5″ climate control touchscreen.

Both also include a native NACS port so that you can access Tesla Superchargers without a separate adapter.

However, the EV6 uses an 800V architecture, enabling faster charging than the EV3, which uses a 400V system.

I've had four EVs and the 800v charging system on my 2025 Ioniq 5 is the biggest improvement I have experienced in any EV. My road trip stops are now about 20 minutes to go from 15% to 85% at fast chargers. To me, this is a game changer. When people talk about range anxiety, they are really talking about long recharging times and with these speeds, you'll be back on the road in the time it takes to hit the restroom and grab a bit to eat.

The EV6 can charge from 10% to 80% in about 18 minutes, whereas the EV3 takes about 30 minutes.

The EV6 is also larger and less boxy than the EV3, measuring 184.8″ long, 74″ wide, and 60.8″ tall, with a 114.2″ wheelbase. In comparison, the EV3 is 169.3″ long, 72.8″ wide, and 62″ tall, with a 105.5″ wheelbase.

Which one would you drive? The new EV3, the EV6, or would you go with Kia’s three-row EV9? Let us know in the comments.

#4728. The Law of Reversed Effort

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

For the better part of this decade, I suffered from a severe case of insomnia. Initially, it had biological origins. After coming down with COVID early in the pandemic, the virus triggered a rare autoimmune condition in me called Morvan syndrome. Morvan’s gift to its victims is profound, treatment-resistant insomnia (agrypnia excitata), and the syndrome can be fatal in up to 20 percent of reported cases. Fortunately (though it’s hard to diagnose), once it’s identified, it’s quite treatable. Unfortunately, prolonged insomnia can develop a learned psychological component, even after the original biological problem improves, so my sleepless nights continued even after IVIG immunotherapy resolved most of the other consequences of the condition.

So, as behavioral scientists often do, I was determined to solve my problem through intellect and science. I bought an Oura Ring and started tracking my sleep. I learned everything I could about sleep hygiene. I hired a sleep coach, therapist, and hypnotherapist. I got a silly pair of glasses and bought all the supplements. I even started injecting myself with peptides purported to help with sleep. Like so many who suffer from insomnia, I just wanted out of it. I jumped the shark when I bought a machine to freeze my prefrontal cortex, a machine so loud my poor wife was now not able to sleep either.

After more than five years of suffering, one little trick made it stop: I decided to stop caring. To be clear, I didn’t suddenly abandon my healthy sleep habits; I just stopped treating good sleep as something I needed to achieve.

If you follow my work, you know Alan Watts has been a significant influence in what I do. Although the law of reversed effort didn’t originate with him, he helped popularize similar ideas through his writing about Taoism and effortless action. Watts even described Lao-tzu as a master of the law of reversed effort.

Despite the name, the law of reversed effort is not a scientific law per se, in the same sense as something found in empirical disciplines. Rather, it’s a psychological idea that there are certain outcomes where increasing conscious effort begins to work against us. Sleep has emerged as the textbook example of this concept, but it shows up in a lot of places. For instance, the paradox of hedonism is the idea that the best way to become unhappy is to chase happiness (the foundation of my book, The Fun Habit). Or the ironic monitoring process, a topic extensively explored by psychologist Daniel Wegner, where in the pursuit of peace of mind, you inadvertently train yourself to subconsciously always scan for threats, therefore making peace of mind elusive.

Here’s how Wegner explains the monitoring process: When we deliberately try to create or suppress a mental state, two processes get activated. One tries to produce the outcome we want; the other monitors whether we are succeeding. Unfortunately, that monitoring process must keep looking for evidence of failure. For instance, if your goal is to stop feeling anxious, some part of your attention must continually ask, “Am I still anxious?”

In my case, with the goal of desperately wanting to fall asleep, my brain (unintentionally) was trained to keep noticing whether I was still awake. In fact, there’s even a sleep treatment that uses this paradox and reverses it. “Paradoxical intention” asks people with insomnia to let go of the effort to force sleep and, in some versions, gently try to stay awake instead. A systematic review and meta-analysis found that paradoxical intention improved important insomnia outcomes and reduced sleep-related performance anxiety (although the authors acknowledged that stronger research in this area is still needed).

For those of us like me who enjoy living in health metrics and data, optimization runs the risk of making problems worse. With sleep trackers now becoming ubiquitous, the problem has become so prevalent that researchers now have a term for it: orthosomnia. But hyperfocusing on a personal problem is hardly unique to sleep.

Both of my parents were professors who lived through the publish-or-perish era. Now that I better understand the pressures of that time, I’ve forgiven them for never being around. However, because there is a lot of residual pain from their absence, I’ve always felt a sense of duty to ensure that my children have all the access to me they need.

So, I read all the good parenting books and followed all the parenting influencers on social media; I tried to be the best parent I could be at every step. But beneath all those good intentions, a practice of rumination and a small “sub-agent of evaluation” began to emerge, framing our interactions as performative. In other words, every interaction with my kids was also an opportunity to collect data. Did I handle that correctly? Was I present enough? And even though I hate to admit this one: Do they like me?

Serendipitously, when my sleep miraculously improved, it dawned on me pretty quickly that I could apply the law of reversed effort to other areas of my life. So, I stopped worrying about being a good father (important to note, I didn’t stop being a good father). I was able to pull this off because I benefited from the confidence of knowing I had enough reps in to trust that the one-off disagreements and difficult afternoons were not a referendum. And once I stopped keeping score, something magical happened: I became more available to what was actually happening. The result is we all started having a lot more fun.

I can already see fans of Ryan Holiday’s work roll their eyes, so let me state the obvious: The law of reversed effort can be problematic if taken too far.Folks who truly know me understand that my argument is never for passivity or living a life of whimsy. On the contrary, direct effort works well for countless things. If you want to become stronger, you need to lift weights. If you want to learn a musical instrument, you need to practice. If you want deeper relationships, you need to put in the time.The important distinction to be aware of is between actions we can perform and states we’re trying to force, as well as becoming comfortable with not being wedded to an outcome. I can create a supportive environment in which to go to bed. I cannot command myself to sleep. I can listen carefully and be present with my children. I cannot force them to be endearing at every turn. I can flex my agency and autonomy to create time for enjoyable experiences. I can only order myself to become happy at my own peril.

Here’s a question I find myself asking more and more these days: Is this something I can directly affect? Or is this something more likely to emerge if I create the right conditions?

If you’ve gotten this far, I hope you see it was never about caring less. It’s about recognizing when your level of caring has quietly turned into an anxiety trap, because you’re trying to control something that is uncontrollable.

Some things respond beautifully when we push harder. Others seem to require us to create the right conditions, loosen our grip, and then simply allow them to happen. Learning this hasn’t just helped me improve my sleep. It’s made my life better by freeing up energy to be fully present with those I love and cherish. I’m excited to see where else I can benefit from the law of reversed effort as I apply it to other areas of my life. Stay tuned.

Ansfield, M. E., Wegner, D. M., & Bowser, R. (1996). Ironic effects of sleep urgency. Behaviour Research and Therapy, 34(7), 523–531. doi:10.1016/0005-7967(96)00031-9.

Baron, K. G., Abbott, S., Jao, N., Manalo, N., & Mullen, R. (2017). Orthosomnia: Are some patients taking the quantified self too far? Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine, 13(2), 351–354. doi:10.5664/jcsm.6472.

Espie, C. A., Broomfield, N. M., MacMahon, K. M., Macphee, L. M., & Taylor, L. M. (2006). The attention-intention-effort pathway in the development of psychophysiologic insomnia: a theoretical review. Sleep Medicine Reviews, 10(4), 215–245. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.smrv.2006.03.002

Jansson-Fröjmark, M., Alfonsson, S., Bohman, B., Rozental, A., & Norell-Clarke, A. (2022). Paradoxical intention for insomnia: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Sleep Research, 31(2), e13464. doi:10.1111/jsr.13464.

Masood, W., Lui, F., & Sitammagari, K. K. (2024). Morvan syndrome. In StatPearls. StatPearls Publishing.

Mauss, I. B., Tamir, M., Anderson, C. L., & Savino, N. S. (2011). Can seeking happiness make people unhappy? Paradoxical effects of valuing happiness. Emotion, 11(4), 807–815. doi:10.1037/a0022010.

Watts, A. W. (1951). The wisdom of insecurity: A message for an age of anxiety. Pantheon Books.

Wegner, D. M. (1994). Ironic processes of mental control. Psychological Review, 101(1), 34–52.
